p122.lead: Gabriel’s choice, two announcements, a noontide birth in Bethlehem, and the flight to Egypt: the first chapter in the story of a universe Son who came to an ordinary home.

p122.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p122.s0.h: Introduction — Why the Home of Joseph and Mary?
p122.s0.b0: The narrator begins by admitting that it is hardly possible to explain fully why Michael chose Palestine, and within it the family of Joseph and Mary. Yet he makes clear that the choice was no impulse but a careful process of several stages, beginning with a review of the Melchizedek report and ending with Gabriel’s personal selection.

head: Stage
Who
What
rows: Michael and Gabriel

Gabriel
Visited Urantia in person, surveyed its peoples spiritually, intellectually, racially, and geographically, and judged the Hebrews to be the bestowal race
The Family Commission of Twelve

Gabriel

p122.s0.b2: This procedure shows that even the affairs of heaven move in an orderly way—by investigation, counsel, and approval. Yet the final choice was made not by the commission’s list but by Gabriel’s own judgment. Paper 122 begins in the home that was prepared in this way.
p122.s1.h: I. Joseph and Mary — A Wide Lineage in an Average Life
p122.s1.b0: Joseph was a Hebrew of the Hebrews, though many non-Jewish strains had entered his line through its women, and his ancestry reached back through Abraham to Andon and Fonta. David and Solomon were not in his direct line; his immediate ancestors were mechanics—builders, carpenters, masons, and smiths. Mary was a Jew in culture and belief, but in hereditary endowment she was more a composite of Syrian, Hittite, Phoenician, Greek, and Egyptian stocks.
p122.s1.b1: Of all couples in Palestine at that time, these two possessed the most ideal combination of widespread racial connections and superior average personality endowments. The standard of choice was not distinction but normality.
p122.s2.h: II. Gabriel Appears to Elizabeth — The Forerunner’s Birth
p122.s2.b1: The priest Zacharias and his wife Elizabeth had long been childless. Late in June of 8 B.C. Gabriel appeared to Elizabeth and announced a son, John, who would be the forerunner of the divine teacher, and told her that her kinswoman Mary would be the mother of the child of promise. Elizabeth kept the secret even from her husband for five months, and Zacharias doubted for weeks until a dream finally convinced him.
p122.s2.b2: Mary visited Elizabeth and stayed three weeks, comparing their experiences, and Elizabeth did much to strengthen Mary’s faith. John was born on March 25, 7 B.C., and from infancy his parents wisely impressed on him the idea that he was to become a spiritual leader. Even a great calling grows within relationships that encourage one another and within the teaching of the home.
p122.s3.h: III–IV. Gabriel’s Announcement to Mary; Joseph’s Dream
p122.s3.b0: One evening about sundown Gabriel appeared to Mary beside a low stone table, told her to call her son Joshua, and said that he would inaugurate the kingdom of heaven. Mary kept this to herself for many weeks; when Joseph heard it, he trusted his wife yet could not sleep for many nights. Mary’s parents and brothers and sisters were always skeptical about Jesus’ mission.
p122.s3.b2: Joseph set aside his doubts only after a dream in which a celestial messenger told him that in the child would be life, and that this life would become the light of mankind. The narrator stresses that none of these visitations said anything about the house of David, about a deliverer of the Jews, or even about the long-expected Messiah. Joseph was counted of the “⟦Q 122:4.2⟧house of David⟦/Q⟧” only because, six generations earlier, an orphaned paternal ancestor had been adopted by Zadoc, a descendant of David.
p122.s3.b4: The text says that most of the so-called Messianic prophecies were applied to Jesus long after his life on earth. “⟦Q 122:4.4⟧A maiden shall bear a son⟦/Q⟧” was made to read “⟦Q 122:4.4⟧a virgin shall bear a son⟦/Q⟧,” and the later genealogies cannot be depended on as factual. Faith must always guard against the temptation to adjust the facts to fit its expectations.
p122.s4.h: V. Jesus’ Earth Parents — Two Temperaments in Harmony
p122.s4.b0: Joseph and Mary were opposite in temperament. Jesus received different gifts from each, and as an adult he more often drove forward in the manner of his mother’s optimistic and determined disposition. Both were good teachers, educated well above the average of their day.

p122.s4.b2: Had Joseph lived, says the narrator, he would surely have become a firm believer in his eldest son’s divine mission. Mary alternated between belief and doubt, swayed by her other children and relatives, but the memory of Gabriel’s appearance right after the conception always steadied her final attitude. Most of Joseph’s family later believed Jesus’ teachings, while very few of Mary’s people did.
p122.s4.b3: Their courtship began when Mary brought Joseph a cup of water during a noontime meal while he was working for her father. They married when Joseph was twenty-one and moved into the new home in Nazareth that he had built with his brothers. The heart of this section is that two very different people formed one home and together nurtured the balanced personality of one child.
p122.s5.h: VI–VII. The Home at Nazareth; The Trip to Bethlehem
p122.s5.b0: The home at Nazareth was a one-room stone house with a flat roof; a low stone table, a loom, a lampstand, and sleeping mats made up most of its furnishings. It stood on the outskirts of the town near the high hill, which later made it easy for Jesus to stroll in the country and climb the hill.
p122.s5.b2: Augustus’s census was taken in Palestine a year late, in 7 B.C. Joseph could have registered for the family alone, but Mary, adventurous and aggressive, insisted on going. They had only one beast of burden, so Mary, large with child, rode while Joseph walked.

p122.s6.h: VIII. The Birth of Jesus — A Noon Without a Star
p122.s6.b0: At noon on August 21, 7 B.C., with the help of women fellow travelers, Mary gave birth to a son, and the babe was laid in a near-by manger. The seraphim sang anthems of glory over the manger, but their praise was not heard by human ears.
p122.s6.b2: The day after the birth Joseph made his enrollment, and through a man they had met at Jericho, a well-to-do friend gladly exchanged his room at the inn with them. On the eighth day the child was circumcised and formally named Joshua. A momentous event of a universe passed quietly, surrounded by the small kindnesses of strangers.
p122.s6.b3: Zacharias, Elizabeth, and Mary believed that Jesus would become the Messiah and successor of David on the throne, and so the family stayed in Bethlehem more than a year. This section draws a clear line between beautiful legend and what actually happened.

head: The familiar story
What the text says
rows: Shepherds came to worship the babe

The star of Bethlehem

p122.s6.b6: The narrator explains that in an age of oral tradition, myths easily became traditions, and traditions came to be accepted as facts. A faith that loves truth treasures what really happened more than a moving story.
p122.s7.h: IX–X. The Presentation in the Temple; Herod Acts
p122.s7.b0: According to the law of Moses, Joseph and Mary went to the temple in Jerusalem to redeem their first-born son and to offer the sacrifice of purification. Simeon the singer and Anna the poetess, who had been told the secret by Zacharias, recognized the child by a prearranged signal, and Simeon sang a song composed by Anna. But on the way back to Bethlehem, Joseph was not in harmony with this premature effort to make Jesus out to be the Jewish Messiah.
p122.s7.b2: A copy of parts of Simeon’s song reached Herod. When more than a year of searching failed to find the child, Herod ordered every boy under two years of age in Bethlehem to be killed. A believer at court warned Zacharias, and the night before the massacre Joseph and Mary left with the babe for Alexandria, where they stayed two full years, until after Herod’s death.
p122.s7.b3: These were hard times for the family. Joseph was afraid to seek work, their small savings were rapidly disappearing, and at the purification ceremony he offered only two young pigeons, as the law directed for poor mothers. Zacharias provided the funds for the flight, and in Alexandria well-to-do relatives of Joseph’s family gave them lodging.
p122.s8.b0: Paper 122 portrays the birth of a universe Son without miraculous decoration. He was born of ordinary parents, in the same way as every other baby, in a granary below a crowded inn. The only supernatural event was Gabriel’s announcement; everything after it unfolded through human faith and doubt, courage and fear.

p122.s8.b2: In Paper 123, “The Early Childhood of Jesus,” the family returns from Alexandria and settles in Nazareth, and the story of the growing child continues.
p123.lead: From Alexandria to Nazareth, from the coming of the Adjuster to the synagogue school: eight years in which a child full of questions grew up among his family and neighbors.

p123.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p123.s0.b0: Paper 123 begins with the family’s refuge in Egypt and follows Jesus until he is eight years old. In Alexandria Joseph soon found work and was promoted to foreman of a large group of workmen on a public building, which gave him the idea of becoming a contractor and builder. That experience would later change the life of the Nazareth family.
p123.s0.b1: At first Mary wanted to keep the child always at her side, but Joseph and their kinsfolk persuaded her that this would deprive him of the helpful experience of learning to get along with children his own age. Mary came to see that undue sheltering might make him self-conscious and self-centered, and she agreed to let the child of promise grow up like any other child. It was the moment when love turned from holding the child close to letting him grow.
p123.s0.b3: The believers in Alexandria urged the family to stay, insisting that the child of destiny would exert a far greater world influence there, and on parting they gave him a complete copy of the Hebrew scriptures in Greek. After they returned to Bethlehem in 4 B.C., Mary still wanted to raise him in the City of David, but Joseph spent three weeks persuading her that Galilee was better for the child’s safety and education.
p123.s1.h: I. Back in Nazareth — A Promise of Silence Kept
p123.s1.b0: On the fourth day of the journey the family reached Nazareth, and for the first time since Jesus’ birth Mary settled down to enjoy life in her own home. Jesus was about three years and two months old. On the way, Joseph and Mary had agreed not to tell anyone in Galilee that Jesus was a child of promise, and they kept that promise faithfully.
p123.s1.b1: In his fourth year Jesus formed a lifelong friendship with a neighbor boy named Jacob. Joseph built a small workshop near the village spring and the caravan tarrying lot, and Jesus grew up listening to the talk of travelers from the four corners of the earth. The family grew as follows.

p123.s2.h: II. The Fifth Year (2 B.C.) — The Adjuster Arrives, and a Boy Full of Questions
p123.s2.b0: On February 11, 2 B.C., when Jesus reached the age of his first personal and wholehearted moral decision, a Thought Adjuster came to dwell with him. This Adjuster had served earlier with Machiventa Melchizedek and so had experience in connection with an incarnation. From that day the direct supervision of the Universe Rulers ended, and Jesus’ guardianship rested with the indwelling Adjuster and the seraphic guardians.
p123.s2.b1: Yet Jesus, like millions of other children, did not notice that moment. The Adjuster came to him quietly, just as it comes to every normal child.
p123.s2.b3: The most valuable part of Jesus’ early education came from his parents’ faithful answers to his questions. Joseph and Mary could not always answer them, but they never failed to help him work toward a satisfying solution of his own.
p123.s2.b5: The Galilean Jews had a systematic program for rearing their children, dividing a child’s life into seven stages. On August 21, 2 B.C., following custom, Mary formally turned Jesus over to Joseph for further instruction.

p123.s2.b7: Even afterward Mary taught him to care for the vines and flowers of the garden, and in shallow boxes of sand on the roof he practiced writing Aramaic, Greek, and later Hebrew. Had you been there, says the narrator, you would only have seen a normal, healthy, and exceedingly inquisitive child.
p123.s3.h: III. Events of the Sixth Year (1 B.C.) — A First Disillusionment and Talks with the Father
p123.s3.b0: Joseph taught Jesus Greek using the scriptures they had received in Egypt. It was one of only two complete copies in Greek in all Nazareth, so a steady stream of truth seekers came to the house. Before he was six, Jesus asked his father the cause of an earthquake, and Joseph honestly answered that he did not know.
p123.s3.b2: Joseph avoided the easy answer of blaming God for the earthquake. Jesus long accepted the doctrine of good and evil spirits as a possible explanation of mental and spiritual phenomena, but very early he doubted that unseen influences caused the physical happenings of nature. An honest “I do not know” opened the child’s thinking in the right direction.
p123.s3.b3: After a visit from John’s family, Jesus took a keen interest in the history of Israel and its feasts, and Joseph explained the meaning of each in turn.

p123.s3.b5: This year Jesus puzzled his parents by insisting on talking to his heavenly Father much as he talked to his earthly father. This intimate conversation, added after his formal prayers, foreshadows the relationship with the Father he would one day proclaim.
p123.s3.b7: Joseph became a builder, and the family income more than trebled; Jesus traveled with his father to the surrounding towns and diligently stored up knowledge about how people lived. Mary was a fairly strict disciplinarian, but Joseph would sit down and explain the reasons behind family rules, and when Jesus understood, he always cooperated willingly.
p123.s4.h: IV. The Seventh Year (A.D. 1) — An Accident That Could Not Be Avoided
p123.s4.b0: The seventh year was eventful. In January came one of the deepest snowfalls at Nazareth in a hundred years. Jewish children of that time mostly played at the serious things their elders did, such as weddings and funerals, and Jesus played with wood blocks in the corner of the carpenter shop. He found it hard to see the harm in certain games forbidden on the Sabbath, but he never went against his parents’ wishes.
p123.s4.b1: Mary used the profits from selling doves as a special charity fund, and Jesus administered it after deducting the tithe and turning it over to the synagogue officer. This small responsibility, given to a seven-year-old, taught generosity with his own hands.
p123.s4.b2: In July of A.D. 1, during an unusual sandstorm, Jesus fell coming down the stone stairs from the roof. A primary and a secondary midwayer had been assigned to watch over him, but the narrator makes clear that the accident was not due to any neglect by the midwayers or the guardian seraphim; it simply could not have been avoided. Afterward Joseph built a balustrade on both sides of the stairway.
p123.s4.b4: Ordinarily only midway creatures can intervene in material conditions, and then only on the specific mandate of their superiors. That even a Son of God was not exempt from ordinary accidents keeps us from reading our own accidents as punishment or abandonment. Frightened, Mary unwisely kept Jesus close at her side for some months.
p123.s5.h: V. School Days in Nazareth — Three Strands of Education
p123.s5.b0: In August of his seventh year Jesus entered the synagogue school, spending three years in the elementary school and three in the advanced school, where the law was learned by repeating it aloud. For his birthday text he chose words from Isaiah.

head: Where
What he gained
rows: His home
Moral training and spiritual culture
The chazan (synagogue teacher)
Intellectual and theological education
His fellows—young and old, Jew and gentile
The equipment of mind and heart for grappling with life’s hard problems: his real education

p123.s5.b4: Nazareth was a caravan way station and a center of liberal interpretation of the law. Jesus spoke freely in Greek with caravan travelers at the spring, and on Sabbath afternoons he climbed the hill with his father to view Mount Carmel, Mount Hermon, the Decapolis, and the Mediterranean. He learned to milk the cow, make cheese, and weave, and his imagination grew beside the wheel of Nathan the potter. The chazan even admitted that he feared he had learned more from Jesus’ searching questions than he had been able to teach him.
p123.s6.h: VI. His Eighth Year (A.D. 2) — A Decision Made with the Father
p123.s6.b0: Jesus was diligent enough to belong to the more progressive third of his class, which earned him one week a month on an uncle’s farm or by the Sea of Galilee. He learned new techniques of numbers from a mathematics teacher from Damascus, and by trading dairy products for lessons he became a skillful harpist by eleven. His questions about the dry and rainy seasons and the difference in temperatures never stopped.
p123.s6.b1: Nahor, a teacher from a rabbinical academy in Jerusalem, came and urged that Jesus be educated in Jerusalem; Mary was half persuaded, and Joseph hesitated. At Nahor’s request the matter was laid before the eight-year-old Jesus, who for two days consulted his parents and a neighbor and talked “⟦Q 123:6.9⟧with my Father who is in heaven⟦/Q⟧,” then answered that he should remain at home.
p123.s6.b2: Joseph was sure his son would be a man of destiny, but profoundly uncertain what that destiny would prove to be, and the more he thought about it, the more he questioned the wisdom of a stay in Jerusalem. With the parents divided, the weight of the decision passed to the child. Jesus felt unequal to the responsibility, yet without hurrying he listened, asked, and prayed, and then decided, though he was not perfectly sure of the answer.
p123.s6.b4: They all marveled, and Nahor returned to Jerusalem. Many years passed before the subject of leaving home came up again. The judgment that those who love us know us better than expert strangers shows a deep trust in the value of the home.
p123.s7.b0: The Jesus of Paper 123 is not a wonder-working child but one who asks, plays, falls, and learns. The Adjuster came quietly, his parents admitted what they did not know, and among family, neighbors, and caravan travelers he learned to understand and love people. The power of this paper lies in showing that a divine life walked the path of ordinary growth.

p123.s7.b2: Paper 124, “The Later Childhood of Jesus,” follows the boy from nine to thirteen, as he slowly becomes aware of his mission.
p124.lead: A forbidden drawing, the games at Scythopolis, a conflict between two commands, and “The hour has come”: a boy from nine to thirteen awakening to who he is.

p124.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p124.s0.h: Introduction — Why Nazareth and Not Alexandria
p124.s0.b0: Paper 124 covers Jesus’ life from his ninth year to his first Passover at thirteen. The narrator begins by noting what it meant for him to grow up in Nazareth. Alexandria might have offered better schooling, but Nazareth gave him something Alexandria could not.

head: Aspect
Had he stayed in Alexandria
What he actually gained in Nazareth
rows: Education
Directed by Jews, along exclusively Jewish lines
A setting for working out his own life problems with a minimum of guidance
Contacts
Constant contact with men and women of all classes from every part of the civilized world
Result
Preparation to understand the gentiles, and a balanced view of the Eastern (Babylonian) and Western (Hellenic) views of Hebrew theology

p124.s0.b2: The insight is that a wider life, more than a better school, forms a person. Most of the events in this paper take place outside school—at home, on the road, and at the caravan shop.
p124.s1.h: I. Jesus’ Ninth Year (A.D. 3) — The Drawing and His First Workbench
p124.s1.b0: Jesus loved drawing landscapes and modeling objects in clay. In late winter he challenged the chazan over the teaching that all images and pictures were idolatrous, and when he was caught drawing a charcoal picture of the teacher on the schoolroom floor, a committee of elders came to Joseph. Resenting their blame of his father, Jesus fearlessly faced his accusers, courageously defended his viewpoint, and with consummate self-control announced that he would abide by his father’s decision.
p124.s1.b1: Joseph ruled that the rabbinical interpretation of the second commandment should prevail, and Jesus never again drew or modeled a likeness while he lived in his father’s house. Giving up a favorite pastime while still unconvinced that he had done wrong was one of the great trials of his young life. When conviction and obedience collided, he chose to state his view plainly while respecting the right to decide.
p124.s1.b2: After Martha was born in September, Joseph built an addition to the workshop, and for the first time Jesus had his own tools and a small workbench. The first ice he ever saw, and the steam escaping from boiling pots, set him thinking a great deal about the constitution of the physical world.
p124.s1.b4: That May he helped with the grain harvest on his uncle’s farm for the first time. Before he was thirteen he had learned something about nearly every kind of work done around Nazareth except metal working, and he often went with his father to Cana, Nain, and Sepphoris, the capital of Galilee. He came to know the lives of working people from the inside.
p124.s1.b5: Before he was ten he had become the leader of seven boys who formed a society for promoting the acquirements of manhood. His trips away from home gave him a more generous understanding of his own family, and by now even his parents were beginning to learn from him.
p124.s2.h: II. The Tenth Year (A.D. 4) — The Boy Who Would Not Fight
p124.s2.b0: On the Sabbath of July 5, A.D. 4, while walking in the country with his father, Jesus first voiced thoughts showing that he was becoming self-conscious of the unusual nature of his mission. The next day he had a longer talk with his mother. Both listened attentively but volunteered no information, and almost two years passed before Jesus raised the subject again.
p124.s2.b1: His playmates saw nothing supernatural in him. He asked more questions than the others, but in most ways he was just like them. In one respect, however, he was different.
p124.s2.b3: He did not suffer much for this trait because Jacob, a neighbor boy a year older, appointed himself Jesus’ defender. Jesus was fair, and he possessed a rare, understanding sympathy that bordered on discreet compassion, so he became the well-loved leader of the boys his age. He loved talking politics and religion with older people, and he turned even play toward more serious channels.
p124.s2.b5: After watching the fishing industry on the lake of Galilee, he nearly decided to become a fisherman; his father’s trade later drew him toward carpentry; and at last a combination of influences led him to choose to become a religious teacher of a new order. His calling was not settled all at once but narrowed through experience.
p124.s3.h: III. The Eleventh Year (A.D. 5) — Scythopolis, and the End of Boyhood
p124.s3.b0: Joseph and Mary were often tempted to show Jesus favoritism or to betray their knowledge that he was a child of promise, but they wisely refrained; on the rare occasions they did show a preference, the boy was quick to refuse it. At the caravan supply shop he gathered an amazing store of information about international affairs.
p124.s3.b1: In May, on a trip with his father to Scythopolis, Jesus was delighted by the orderliness of the Greek city and thrilled by the games in the amphitheater. That night, when he suggested building an amphitheater at Nazareth, Joseph for the first and only time grew angry with his son and told him never to say such a thing again.
p124.s3.b3: Jesus kept that promise as long as his father lived. Yet he did not give up the idea of wholesome recreation, and later he tried to bring it, as far as Jewish practice allowed, into the program of his twelve apostles. Obedience need not mean abandoning an idea; it can mean waiting for its time.
p124.s3.b4: On June 24 Jude, the seventh child, was born, and Mary was very ill for several weeks. Just before he turned eleven, Jesus took on the responsibilities of the first-born son a year or two early. From the end of this year he gave himself more and more to deep meditation on how to keep both his obligations to his family and his mission to the world.
p124.s4.h: IV. The Twelfth Year (A.D. 6) — A Dual Nature, and Two Great Commands
p124.s4.b0: Jesus began working regularly in the carpenter shop and was permitted to manage his own earnings, and he learned the discretion of concealing whatever might make him seem different from others. This year he went through many seasons of uncertainty, if not actual doubt, about the nature of his mission. It was hard to recognize a double origin within a single personality.
p124.s4.b2: His parents increasingly realized that something superhuman resided in their son, but they never knew that he was the creator of the local universe. Jesus inclined more and more toward his father’s spiritual view, and Mary was hurt as she sensed her guidance being set aside. This breach of understanding widened with the years.
p124.s4.b4: From this time on he grew more tactful and considerate with his brothers and sisters. He always got along well with James, Miriam, and Martha; his difficulties at home came mainly from friction with Joseph and Jude, particularly Jude. He taught the home school for his siblings, and because the Nazareth synagogue was under a liberal school of rabbis, he was able to modify religious forms such as the family prayers.
p124.s4.b5: He did not fully understand the ban on images, but with his high concept of consistency he pointed out that kissing the doorpost parchment was idolatrous by the same logic, and Joseph removed the parchment. Above all, he was torn between two great commands.

head: The two commands
Wording
The harmony Jesus found
rows: Loyalty to conviction
“Be loyal to the dictates of your highest convictions of truth and righteousness.”
He never shirked the necessary daily adjustments
Honor to parents
“Honor your father and mother, for they have given you life and the nurture thereof.”
He blended them into a concept of group solidarity based on loyalty, fairness, tolerance, and love

p124.s5.h: V. His Thirteenth Year (A.D. 7) — Graduation and Assurance
p124.s5.b0: In January of A.D. 7 his baby brother Amos was born. About the middle of February Jesus became humanly assured that he was destined to perform a mission on earth for the enlightenment of man and the revelation of God. Outwardly he was an average Jewish boy, but far-reaching plans were forming in his mind.
p124.s5.b2: On March 20 he graduated from the synagogue school and was pronounced a “⟦Q 124:5.4⟧son of the commandment⟦/Q⟧.” The elders made plans to send him to the academies in Jerusalem, but Jesus grew more and more sure he would never go. His father’s approaching death and the support of a large family would soon change all such plans.
p124.s6.h: VI. The Journey to Jerusalem — “The Hour Has Come”
p124.s6.b0: Now graduated, Jesus set out with his parents in a company of 103 to attend his first Passover. They avoided Samaria by going down the Jordan valley, and along the way he heard the old stories of Israel.

head: Day
Places passed
What to remember

Shunem, Jezreel, Mount Gilboa
Scythopolis seen in the distance; Mary knew nothing of the previous year’s dispute
Second day

Recollections of Gideon’s day; Herod’s fortress of Alexandrium

Villages built by Herod, Jericho

Mount of Olives, Bethany, Jerusalem
The beginning of a lifelong friendship with Lazarus’s family

p124.s6.b3: In Jerusalem the family stayed at the home of a well-to-do relative of Mary’s. Amid the busy preparations Joseph took his son to visit the academy where he was to continue his studies at fifteen, but he was puzzled at how little interest Jesus showed in these careful plans. The boy’s heart was already turned elsewhere.
p124.s6.b4: Deeply impressed by the temple services, he asked fewer questions than at any time since he was four, absorbed in his own meditations. He did ask why so many innocent animals had to be slaughtered, and his father’s answers did not satisfy him. On the day before the Passover Sabbath, affectionate pity for the spiritually blind multitudes filled his heart, and that night, for the first time, a messenger commissioned by Immanuel appeared to him.
p124.s6.b6: This visit, which came even before the heavy burdens of the family fell on him, announced that the hour had come to resume the responsibilities of a universe. It was the first act in a long series of events that culminated in the completion of the bestowal. The narrator confesses that even for the midwayers the mystery grew deeper over time.
p124.s7.b0: Paper 124 shows divine self-consciousness slowly emerging within the ordinary growth of a boy. He gave up drawing, set aside his dream of an amphitheater, and suffered between two commands, yet he never avoided his duty. So ends the career of the Nazareth lad, and so begins the story of a youth striving to integrate his expanding life purpose with his obligations to his family.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Speak your view with courage, but respect a rightful decision
The drawing incident and his father’s ruling
Put relationships and peace ahead of your own rights

Obey, yet keep a good idea alive until its time
Recreation in the apostles’ program
Harmonize conviction and family duty through daily adjustment

Let worship stir compassion for the crowd

p124.s7.b2: Paper 125, “Jesus at Jerusalem,” tells what happened in the temple that Passover week and of the three days the boy stayed behind without his parents.
p125.lead: A first Passover, the temple’s beauty and its spiritual ugliness, three days of teaching by questions, and “I will await my hour”: a twelve-year-old in Jerusalem.

p125.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p125.s0.h: Introduction — A First Taste of Freedom, and a First Disillusionment
p125.s0.b0: The narrator says that no incident in Jesus’ earth career was more engaging or more humanly thrilling than this first visit to Jerusalem. The days after the Passover were the first complete freedom from responsibility he had ever known, and many years would pass before he enjoyed such freedom again. He virtually refused to go unless his mother came too, and so this company had more women, in proportion to men, than any Passover company that had ever left Nazareth.
p125.s0.b1: Seen from the Mount of Olives, the temple was all he had hoped for, but once he entered its gates the disillusionment began. The first shock came when his mother left for the women’s gallery and could not attend his consecration. He was thoroughly indignant at this unjust discrimination, yet apart from a few words of protest to his father he said nothing—though he thought, and thought deeply. The consecration rituals seemed perfunctory and routine, and he missed the personal warmth of the synagogue at Nazareth.
p125.s0.b2: Jesus would never accept explanations of worship that involved the wrath of God or the anger of the Almighty. When his father pressed him to accept orthodox beliefs, he looked into his father’s eyes and reasoned from the love of his earthly father to the love of the heavenly Father.
p125.s0.b4: Joseph and Mary held their peace and never again tried to change his mind about the love of God. In this short answer, which starts from the love of earthly parents and reasons upward to the love of the heavenly Father, his understanding of God is already plain.
p125.s1.h: I. Jesus Views the Temple — Beauty and Spiritual Ugliness
p125.s1.b0: Throughout the temple courts Jesus was shocked by a spirit of irreverence unfit for “⟦Q 125:1.1⟧his Father’s house.⟦/Q⟧” In the court of the gentiles, the din of the money-changers and vendors gave him the shock of his young life, and the sight of courtesans parading within the temple precincts outraged his sense of propriety.

head: Place
What he saw
Jesus’ response
rows: The temple precincts
Vast buildings holding over two hundred thousand worshipers
More intrigued by the spiritual meaning of the ceremonies than by the buildings
The court of the gentiles
Money-changers, sellers of sacrificial animals, cursing and noise
The shock of his young life
Within the temple precinct
Painted courtesans

The priests’ court
Bloodstained pavement, the priests’ gory hands, dying animals
Sickened, he begged to be taken away

p125.s1.b3: Joseph wisely led his son to see the “gate beautiful” and then walked outside with Mary, talking about the feasts. But Jesus had had enough for one visit. A love of beauty and symbol, and an eye that could see through to the emptiness behind form, were awakening together in one boy.
p125.s2.h: II. Jesus and the Passover — Dreaming of a Bloodless Feast
p125.s2.b0: Jesus persuaded his parents to keep the Passover with the family of Simon of Bethany. Asked, as a new son of the covenant, to recount the origin of the Passover, he did it well, but he disconcerted his parents by weaving in impressions of what he had recently seen and heard.
p125.s2.b2: He became more and more determined someday to establish a bloodless Passover. That night he hardly slept for dreams of slaughter, his heart torn by the inconsistencies of the whole ceremonial system. His parents also slept little but feared to talk frankly with him. The narrator adds that Jesus would gladly have talked if they had dared to encourage him. Opening the door to conversation is often the adult’s task.
p125.s2.b3: From the next day, guided by Lazarus, he explored Jerusalem and spent most of his time at the teaching conferences near the temple. On Wednesday night at Bethany, Lazarus, Martha, and Mary heard him speak of things temporal and eternal and from then on loved him as their own brother. He talked with more than one hundred and fifty boys his age, learned how people lived across the world, and began to wish to travel the world himself.
p125.s2.b4: All through Passover week, as a new son of the commandment, he had to sit outside the rail that separated full citizens, so he held back the questions surging in his mind until the feast was over. Again and again his parents found him sitting alone with his head in his hands, but not knowing how troubled his spirit was, they did not know what to do. Before leaving they made definite arrangements for him to return at fifteen to study at a famous rabbinical academy, but they were distressed by his indifference during their visits to the school.
p125.s3.h: III–IV. Departure of Joseph and Mary; First and Second Days in the Temple
p125.s3.b0: On the first day of the week after the festival, the party set out, the men in one group and the women in another. Jesus was so absorbed in a temple discussion about angels that he forgot the time of departure. Mary assumed he was with the men and Joseph thought he was with the women, so they did not discover his absence until they reached Jericho.

head: Day
Jesus
Joseph and Mary
rows: First day

Second day

Searched all day, beginning at their relatives’ house, and found no trace
Third day

Fourth day
Invited by the leader to sit beside him and give his views on prayer and worship

p125.s3.b2: With the crowds gone, the temple had a quieter and more decorous atmosphere. On the second day Jesus boldly asked questions, yet always in a manner consistent with his youth. His pointed questions sometimes embarrassed the teachers of the law, but because he showed candid fairness and an evident hunger for knowledge, most of them treated him with every consideration.
p125.s3.b3: When he questioned the justice of putting to death a drunken gentile who had wandered into the forbidden precincts, an intolerant teacher demanded his age, and the teachers mocked, “⟦Q 125:4.3⟧he is from Nazareth.⟦/Q⟧” But the leader ruled that the boy was not to blame and could continue in the discussions. That night, again, he meditated and prayed in the garden at Bethany.
p125.s4.h: V. The Third Day in the Temple — Teaching by Questions
p125.s4.b0: On the third day word had spread and many spectators gathered; Simon too came down from Bethany. Before the day ended, the entire attention of the chief discussion group was focused on his questions. The text records five of them.

head: Question
The issue behind it
rows: 1. What really exists in the holy of holies, behind the veil?
Symbol and reality in ritual
2. Why should the mothers in Israel be segregated from the male worshipers?
Discrimination in worship
3. If God is a loving Father, why all this slaughter of animals?
The sacrificial system and the teaching of Moses
4. Is it consistent to permit barter and trade where the Father is worshiped?
The commercialization of the temple
5. Is the Messiah a temporal prince on David’s throne, or the light of life in a spiritual kingdom?
The concept of the Messiah

p125.s4.b3: Rather than refuting his elders, he challenged their teaching and suggested his own through the questions themselves. His manner combined sagacity and humor, endearing him even to those who resented his youth, and he was always fair and considerate. This reluctance to take unfair advantage of an opponent marked his entire public ministry.
p125.s4.b5: That evening on Olivet he did not weep; he only bowed his head in silent devotion. Late into the night in the garden he tried to work out a definite plan for freeing his countrymen from their bondage to tradition, but no answer came.
p125.s5.h: VI. The Fourth Day in the Temple — “I Will Await My Hour”
p125.s5.b0: Strangely, Jesus seemed not to grasp how worried his parents would be. On the afternoon of the fourth day, just as the leader had seated him at his side and asked his views on prayer and worship, his parents found him. Mary upbraided him before everyone, and the narrator says this brought an inglorious end to one of the greatest opportunities he would ever have as a teacher of truth.
p125.s5.b1: Earlier that morning the teachers had marveled at his familiarity with the Scriptures in Hebrew as well as Greek, though they were amazed more by his youth than by his knowledge of truth. Before judging the scene, the narrator asks us to remember that Jesus was by then regarded as a young man—a son of the law and a consecrated citizen of Israel.
p125.s5.b3: When the crowd had withdrawn, he first relieved his parents’ embarrassment. His maturity shows in a single sentence that blames no one.
p125.s5.b5: On the way home, on the brow of Olivet, he lamented that Jerusalem was enslaved to the Roman yoke and to its own traditions and cried out that he would return to cleanse the temple. Once home, he assured his parents of his affection and implied that he would never again cause them such anxiety.
p125.s5.b7: On the three-day journey back to Nazareth Jesus said little, and his parents said little too. They could not understand their first-born son, but they treasured his sayings in their hearts.
p125.s5.b9: Mary, however, took the cry on Olivet as a prophecy of her son’s mission as Israel’s deliverer, and with the help of her brother she began to steer his thoughts into patriotic and nationalistic channels. The scene shows how the same words can be read in entirely different ways, according to the hearer’s expectations.
p125.s6.b0: Paper 125 shows a boy holding to God as a loving Father in the very center of institutional religion. He was indignant but never rude; he questioned but never sought to win; he sensed his calling but did not abandon his family. The conclusion of the paper is that he kept both the will of his heavenly Father and obedience to his earthly father, and waited for his hour.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Reason from the love you have known to the love of God
The heavenly Father cannot love less than an earthly father

Teaching conveyed by questions
When misunderstood, ease the situation without blaming anyone

Keep your duties and wait for your time, even when your calling is clear
“I will await my hour”

p125.s6.b2: In Paper 126, “The Two Crucial Years,” the boy returns to Nazareth, his father Joseph dies, and Jesus becomes the head of the family.
p126.lead: The sudden death of Joseph, a fourteen-year-old head of the family, the Lord’s Prayer and “the Son of Man,” a first synagogue sermon: the two most crucial years of testing in Jesus’ life.

p126.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p126.s0.h: Introduction — The Two Most Crucial Years
p126.s0.b0: The narrator calls the fourteenth and fifteenth years the most crucial and most trying of Jesus’ earth life. He had become self-conscious of divinity and destiny, but he had not yet achieved a large measure of communication with his indwelling Thought Adjuster. No youth passing through the confusions of adolescence, says the text, ever faced a more crucial testing.
p126.s0.b2: When her son came back from Jerusalem, Mary hoped he would now be more responsive to her plans, but she was soon more completely disillusioned. The boy spent more and more time with his father, and his parents could not understand how he moved back and forth between the affairs of this world and his Father’s business.
p126.s0.b4: Jesus respected sincere Pharisees and honest scribes but held hypocritical religious leaders in contempt, and his righteous resentment of the politically appointed priests grew. At times he was tempted to look with favor on becoming the Messiah of Jewish expectation, but he never yielded. Meanwhile, the people of Nazareth, hearing of his exploits in the temple, predicted that he would become a great teacher.
p126.s1.h: I. His Fourteenth Year (A.D. 8) — A Future That Looked Bright
p126.s1.b0: At fourteen Jesus was a good yoke maker, skilled with canvas and leather, and fast becoming an expert carpenter and cabinetmaker. He often climbed the hill of Simeon northwest of Nazareth to pray and meditate, gazing on Megiddo and Taanach, Dothan, Ebal and Gerizim, and recalling the history of his father’s people. There he was gradually becoming more self-conscious of the nature of his bestowal.
p126.s1.b1: Joseph set aside property income for Jesus’ studies in Jerusalem the following year. Yet his parents frequently doubted their son’s destiny. The devout people of that day believed that men of promise proved their calling by miracles and wonders, but nothing extraordinary or miraculous ever happened to Jesus. Scores of times his mother waited breathlessly, only to have her hopes dashed.
p126.s1.b2: Still, the family’s finances improved, and Jesus resumed his harp lessons. The narrator sums up the year this way.
p126.s2.h: II. The Death of Joseph — Head of the Family at Fourteen
p126.s2.b0: On September 25, A.D. 8, word came that Joseph had been severely injured by a falling derrick while working on the governor’s residence at Sepphoris. Mary hurried there with James, but Joseph died before she arrived. The family never heard his farewell or his last blessing.
p126.s2.b1: Coming just when the future looked brightest, this blow demolished every plan for study in Jerusalem. A boy just past fourteen now had to carry, along with his heavenly Father’s commission, the care of his widowed mother, seven brothers and sisters, and another yet to be born. The narrator judges these responsibilities heavy but highly educational and disciplinary.
p126.s2.b3: Jesus cheerfully accepted these responsibilities and carried them faithfully to the end. Ironically, the problem of going to the rabbinical academy was now settled. He was willing to learn from anyone, but he never took his authority to teach from men.
p126.s2.b5: The narrator adds that Jesus still knew nothing of Gabriel’s visit to his mother before his birth; he learned of it only from John on the day of his baptism. He was finding his way through his own experience and reflection, not through heavenly announcements. That winter the neighbors would drop in during the evenings to hear him play the harp, tell stories, and read from the Greek scriptures. A grieving home became a small gathering place for the village.
p126.s2.b6: As the years passed, he measured every institution of society and every religious usage by one unvarying test. He gave his time and energy more and more to two purposes: the care of his family and preparation to do his Father’s will. Joseph had left a sum of money, so at first the household ran smoothly, and Jesus proved a liberal but frugal administrator of his father’s estate.

head: Jesus’ test question
What it asks
rows: What does it do for the human soul?
The fruit of an institution or practice
Does it bring God to man?
Whether it is a channel of revelation
Does it bring man to God?
Whether it opens the path of ascent

p126.s3.h: III. The Fifteenth Year (A.D. 9) — The Lord’s Prayer and “the Son of Man”
p126.s3.b0: In April of A.D. 9 Ruth, the baby of the family, was born, and for almost twenty years Jesus loved and nurtured her and the other children as faithfully as any father. Their savings were nearly gone, and they had to dispose of one of the houses that Joseph owned in partnership with his neighbor Jacob.
p126.s3.b1: He tried to lead his brothers and sisters to pray spontaneously, each in his own words, but the children simply took the suggestive phrases he offered as their prayer. At last, one evening in October, by the little lamp on the low stone table, he wrote out a standard family prayer in charcoal on a cedar board. The prayer later known as “⟦Q 126:3.3⟧The Lord’s Prayer⟦/Q⟧” was first formulated in this way, at the family altar.
p126.s3.b2: His family responsibilities removed all thought of immediately beginning his Father’s business. He rightly reasoned that the care of his earthly father’s family must be his first obligation. Meanwhile he pondered deeply who he was and what he should be called.

head: Identity considered
Jesus’ conclusion
rows: The Messiah the Jews expected
Firmly convinced he was not that Messiah; he would not lead armies or sit on David’s throne
A deliverer or moral teacher for the Jews alone
He did not see his mission that way
The Son of Man depicted by Daniel
Certain he would never appear as such
The “Son of Man” of the Book of Enoch
The story of one who walked with the Father in glory and came down to proclaim salvation was nearest the truth; he adopted it as his inaugural title

p126.s3.b4: He knew that the Book of Enoch was not written by Enoch of old and that it mixed in Eastern mysticism. Even so, he recognized and embraced the truth it contained. He looked to the truth of the content rather than to the source.
p126.s3.b6: By now he had settled many things about his coming work for the world, but he said nothing of them to his mother, who still held that he was the Jewish Messiah. The essence of the mission he had settled on was “⟦Q 126:3.10⟧to be about his Father’s business⟦/Q⟧”—to show forth his Father’s loving nature to all mankind.
p126.s3.b7: Yet great confusion followed. To what did the Messianic prophecies refer? Could his mother be right after all? What should be his relation to the Jewish commonwealth, to Rome, and to the gentiles? He pondered each question while making a living at the carpenter’s bench for his mother and eight younger brothers and sisters. Mary was uneasy about his strange ideas, and he learned not to disclose all his thoughts. Outwardly he became ordinary, but he longed for a friend in whom he could confide.
p126.s4.h: IV. First Sermon in the Synagogue — The Chosen Words Were the Message
p126.s4.b0: On the first Sabbath after his fifteenth birthday Jesus conducted the morning service of the Nazareth synagogue for the first time. Instead of commenting, he read a selection of scriptures, and the choice itself became his message: the words about being anointed to bring good news to the meek, the call to cease doing evil and learn to do good, and the charge to defend the fatherless and plead for the widow.
p126.s4.b2: This passage, which asks for justice, mercy, and humility in place of sacrifices, matches the conviction of the boy who had been sickened by the slaughter in the temple. Last he read of the Creator who gives power to the weak and of the promise “fear not.” The townspeople had never seen him so solemn and so authoritative. That afternoon he climbed the hill with James and, on returning, wrote out the Ten Commandments in Greek on two boards.
p126.s5.h: V. The Financial Struggle — An Idealism That Did Not Break
p126.s5.b0: Gradually the family returned to a simple life. A carpenter’s wages fell, so that working early and late Jesus could earn only about twenty-five cents a day, and the tax collector even threatened to take his harp. The great shock of his fifteenth year came when Herod ruled that nothing was due Joseph at his death.

head: Difficulty
Jesus’ response
rows: Savings exhausted
A house was sold; Mary turned the dove business over to James; more cows were bought and milk was sold
Pressure from the tax collector
Fearing it would be seized, he gave his Greek scriptures to the synagogue library as his coming-of-age offering
Herod’s unjust decision
He gave up the dream of buying a small farm and never again trusted Herod Antipas
Loss of contact with caravan travelers
He sent James to the camel lot to gather news of the world
The dream of country life
He rented land north of the house, where the children kept gardens and raised animals

p126.s5.b2: In these years he came to understand almost completely how people of his day lived. That intimate grasp of life in home, field, and workshop shows clearly in his later teaching. The Nazareth chazan still believed he would become a great teacher, perhaps the successor of Gamaliel.
p126.s5.b3: To all appearances, every plan for his career had been thwarted. But he did not falter and was not discouraged; day by day he did the present duty well.
p126.s5.b5: The narrator sees the hard experience of supporting the family as a protection, leaving no room for idle meditation or mysticism. As a thoroughly practical idealist, Jesus met his situation as he found it and did all he could to satisfy his family’s longings as fully as possible.
p126.s6.b0: Paper 126 shows a real life beginning in the place where plans have collapsed. When the fifteenth year closed, the growth period of mind and body had ended, and the real career of this young man began. He passed through those years with faithfulness instead of miracles, responsibility instead of escape, and daily duty instead of discouragement.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Keep loving and being loved even when you are not understood
Parents who did not understand him but truly loved him
Accept a responsibility that falls on you suddenly, and do so willingly
Jesus became head of the family at fourteen
Judge institutions and practices by what they do for the soul
The three test questions
Embrace truth for its content, not its source
The “Son of Man” found in the Book of Enoch
When plans fail, do today’s duty faithfully
The comfort of disappointed idealists

p126.s6.b2: Paper 127, “The Adolescent Years,” follows Jesus from sixteen to twenty as the young head of his family.
p127.lead: From sixteen to twenty: five years in which the young head of a poor, large family passed through political temptation and a declaration of love and grew into full manhood.

p127.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p127.s0.b0: Paper 127 covers Jesus’ sixteenth through twentieth years. Within a few years of his father’s death all the family property was gone, and the eldest son became the head and sole support of a large family. At the same time he grew more and more conscious of his pre-existence and of his purpose: to reveal his Paradise Father to the children of men.
p127.s0.b2: The narrator states the meaning of these years at the outset. Having actually lived through adolescence on a world beset by evil and distraught by sin, the Son of Man became the understanding refuge for the distressed and perplexed adolescents of all the worlds of Nebadon. This paper, then, is both the story of a great life’s growing years and good news for struggling young people today: there is One who knows them.
p127.s1.h: I. The Sixteenth Year (A.D. 10) — Full Growth of Body and Mind
p127.s1.b0: This year Jesus attained his full physical growth and the fullness of capacity for intellectual development. The text describes him carefully, noting that even in the most commonplace contacts there appeared the touch of a twofold nature, the human and the divine.

head: Area
Jesus at sixteen
rows: Body
Healthy and well-proportioned; a virile and comely youth
Mind
Keen and analytical
Disposition
Kind and sympathetic
Temperament
Somewhat fluctuating but aggressive
Impression
A combination of the sympathizing friend and the authoritative teacher

p127.s1.b2: Yet his family understood him less and less. Mary had given them to understand that he was destined to be the deliverer of the Jewish people, so the more frankly Jesus denied such ideas, the more confused they became. Knowing that his mission was so unusual that no one on earth could advise him about it, he spoke of it less and less.
p127.s1.b3: Even so, because the synagogue school would not receive girls, he conducted a home school so that his sisters could learn just as the boys did. He spent the year almost confined to the workbench, yet he was a real, though youthful, father to the family.
p127.s1.b4: Mary grieved to see her son toiling at the carpenter’s bench instead of studying with the rabbis in Jerusalem. But though she could not understand him fully, she loved him, and she appreciated most of all the willing way he shouldered the responsibility of the home. Love and responsibility can walk together even where understanding is lacking.
p127.s2.h: II. The Seventeenth Year (A.D. 11) — The Zealots’ Call, and “Money Cannot Love”
p127.s2.b0: Amid agitation against paying taxes to Rome, a nationalist party arose that would soon be called the Zealots. When its organizers came to Nazareth to see Jesus, he listened carefully and asked many questions but refused to join. His mother, his uncle, and even his brother James urged him to enlist, and Isaac, a wealthy moneylender, offered to support his family if he would lead the Nazareth patriots.
p127.s2.b1: The narrator explains why this was so delicate. Patriotic issues tangled with tax-gathering foreign oppressors are always difficult for spiritual leaders, and doubly so here because the Jewish religion itself was involved in the agitation against Rome. Mary’s brother Simon had already joined and later became an officer, and for several years Jesus and his uncle were estranged.
p127.s2.b2: For the first time Jesus had to resort consciously to public strategy, because he could not reveal that he was more than a man or disclose his future mission. With counsel from his old teacher, the chazan, he stated his position bravely and diplomatically, holding to his first duty to his family.
p127.s2.b4: An unscheduled speech by James disarmed the remaining opposition, and the crisis passed. But Nazareth remained divided about the Son of Man, and this was one of the chief reasons he later moved to Capernaum. That same year Jesus made great progress in bringing his divine and human natures together, accomplishing it by the force of his own decisions with only the aid of his indwelling Monitor.
p127.s3.h: III. The Eighteenth Year (A.D. 12) — Passover with James, and the Death of Amos
p127.s3.b0: All the family property except the home and garden was disposed of. With the pressure eased for a time, Jesus took James to the Passover. On the brow of Olivet, while James exclaimed in wonder at the temple, Jesus gazed on Jerusalem in silence, and in the temple discussions he asked no questions. To his disappointed brother he only replied, “⟦Q 127:3.5⟧My hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧”
p127.s3.b1: In September Elizabeth and John came to visit. After many intimate talks, the two young men agreed not to see each other again until they met in public service when the heavenly Father should call them. In December little Amos died of a high fever, and the cost of a funeral on top of everything else staggered the family. In this sorrow Mary at last recognized Jesus as the real head of the family in the fullest sense.
p127.s3.b3: The narrator says that his sturdy, practical optimism was contagious and helped form strong and noble characters in the children despite the depressiveness of poverty. With his power to concentrate on one problem and his untiring patience, he lived as if “⟦Q 127:3.15⟧seeing Him who is invisible.⟦/Q⟧” This scene shows that hope is not something that comes after circumstances improve; it is the strength to endure them.
p127.s3.b4: Back in Nazareth he worked in the old repair shop he was buying back and was greatly cheered to meet people from all over the country. The text says he truly loved people—just common folks. In the synagogue he arranged the order of readings so that one passage would illuminate another, and whenever the weather permitted he took his brothers and sisters on Sabbath-afternoon nature strolls. By joining the chazan’s young men’s club for philosophic discussion, he regained some of the standing he had lost in the nationalist controversy.
p127.s4.h: IV. The Nineteenth Year (A.D. 13) — The Father-Brother’s Home Training
p127.s4.b0: This year Jesus fully won his mother over to training the children by the positive injunction to do good rather than by the older method of forbidding evil. At home and throughout his public career he always exhorted in the form “⟦Q 127:4.2⟧You shall do this⟦/Q⟧,” and prayer time became the occasion for discussing everything that concerned the family’s welfare.

head: Principle
In practice
rows: Positive exhortation
Commands to do good in place of taboos
Early discipline

Elastic fairness

p127.s4.b3: The text sketches the character of each of the seven children, showing how differently they grew up under the same father-brother. Jesus never disciplined them arbitrarily, and the children, especially the girls, confided their troubles to him as they would to an affectionate father.

head: Sibling

rows: James

Joseph

Jude

Miriam

Martha

Ruth

p127.s4.b5: Jesus gradually liberalized family practices such as Sabbath observance, and Mary gave hearty assent. When Jude started school this year, Jesus sold his harp, his last recreational pleasure, to pay the expenses—comforting himself that at least the harp was now safe from seizure by the tax collector.
p127.s5.h: V. Rebecca, the Daughter of Ezra — A Declaration of Love Declined
p127.s5.b0: Rebecca, the eldest daughter of Ezra, a wealthy merchant of Nazareth, fell in love with Jesus. When Mary and Miriam tried to dissuade her by telling of their belief that he was a son of destiny, her resolve only grew, and her father supported her, offering to compensate the family for the loss of Jesus’ earnings.
p127.s5.b1: Jesus replied that no amount of money could take the place of his personal obligation to rear his father’s family. Through this he faced for the first time the question of marriage, which every average human being must confront. He sincerely thanked Rebecca for her admiration but explained that he was not free to enter into any relationship beyond brotherly regard and pure friendship.
p127.s5.b4: Rebecca moved to Sepphoris, but she waited for him all her life, followed him devotedly during his public career, and stood among the women by the cross. His refusal did not end her love; it turned it into a greater devotion.
p127.s6.h: VI. His Twentieth Year (A.D. 14) — A Passover Without a Lamb, at the Threshold of Manhood
p127.s6.b0: At Passover this year in Bethany, Jesus celebrated the feast with Lazarus, Martha, and Mary without the paschal lamb. He taught that the Father in heaven was not truly concerned with such meaningless rituals and served them unleavened bread and wine as “⟦Q 127:6.7⟧the bread of life⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 127:6.7⟧the water of life⟦/Q⟧.” At home, however, he continued to keep the Passover with his family according to the law of Moses.
p127.s6.b2: When Mary asked him about marriage, he answered that all such things must await “my hour,” and he had already settled in his mind that he would not become the father of children in the flesh. The paper then lists in turn what the twenty-year-old Jesus was learning.

head: What he was learning
Meaning
rows: Bearing responsibility
Carrying on in the face of disappointment
Fairness
Being fair and just even in the face of injustice
Adjusting ideals to reality
Fitting spiritual ideals to the practical demands of earthly life
Near and distant goals
Working for immediate needs while planning for a higher goal
Using spiritual drive
Turning the mechanism of material achievement
A double fatherhood
Depending on the heavenly Father while guiding his earth family

p127.s6.b5: As a child he accumulated knowledge; as a youth he sorted and correlated it; and now as a man he begins to organize these mental possessions for his future teaching and service. Full of sympathy for the frailties of human nature, he prepares for his mission of revealing God to men and leading men to God.
p127.s7.b0: The Jesus of Paper 127 is not a wonder-working youth but a young man who grows by choosing day after day amid poverty, misunderstanding, and temptation. All that human experience became the eternal possession of the Universe Sovereign, and so he became our understanding brother and sympathetic friend.

p127.s7.b2: In Paper 128, “Jesus’ Early Manhood,” he continues to care for his family while beginning, as the Son of Man, to meet the wider world.
p128.lead: From twenty-one to twenty-six: the Son of Man hands the headship of the family to his brothers, declines honors from Damascus and Alexandria, and prepares to leave home.

p128.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p128.s0.h: Introduction — A Creator Living an Ordinary Human Life
p128.s0.b0: Paper 128 covers Jesus’ twenty-first through twenty-sixth years. The narrator first reminds us that he came into the world as other children do, without selecting his parents, and grew up wrestling with the vicissitudes of his environment just like other mortals. He then sets out two purposes we must always keep in mind when reading of this bestowal.

head: Purpose of Michael’s bestowal
Meaning
rows: 1. Mastering experience
Living the full life of a human creature in mortal flesh, completing his sovereignty in Nebadon
2. Revealing the Father
Revealing the Universal Father to the mortals of time and space and leading them to a better understanding of him
Incidental
Benefits to other creatures and advantages to the universe

p128.s0.b2: These two purposes are the thread running through the whole paper. Each ordinary scene—caring for the family, working, declining offers, training his brothers—was at once experience that earned sovereignty and a life that revealed the Father.
p128.s1.h: I. The Twenty-First Year (A.D. 15) — A True Man Among Men
p128.s1.b0: Having reached adulthood, Jesus began in earnest, fully aware of his dual nature, to complete the experience of living the life of his lowest form of intelligent creatures. He labored, grew weary, rested, and slept; he hungered and thirsted and experienced the full range of human feelings. He chose “⟦Q 128:1.2⟧the Son of Man⟦/Q⟧” as his first title because he knew full well that he was a mortal man, born of woman.
p128.s1.b2: As to the attributes of his prehuman existence he emptied himself, and before his public work his knowledge of men and events was wholly self-limited. So, as one who was actually tested and tried, he is abundantly able to understand and minister to the confused and distressed. That we have a ruler who knows our weakness is the first comfort this paper offers its readers.
p128.s1.b4: His human nature was self-evident to him, but the self-realization of his divine nature was a slow and natural evolutionary revelation. It began in Jerusalem when he was nearly thirteen and was completed at his baptism in the Jordan, and nothing supernatural happened in between. The narrator testifies that, apart from his guardian seraphim, he did not use the guidance of celestial personalities.
p128.s1.b5: This does not mean he was not divine. After he began his public career, he made no objection when he was called by many great titles. There was only one title he refused.
p128.s1.b7: At Passover this year he took his brother Joseph to Jerusalem, because he never showed partiality in his family. When Joseph asked about his mission along the way, he usually replied only, “⟦Q 128:1.15⟧My hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧”
p128.s2.h: II. The Twenty-Second Year (A.D. 16) — James Installed as Acting Head
p128.s2.b0: As his brothers and sisters passed one by one through the trials of adolescence, Jesus grappled with their problems alongside them. A family conference decided that not all the boys should become carpenters, and Simon went to work with Jacob the stone mason. When carpentry was slack, Jesus went to Sepphoris and spent six months learning the smith’s trade.
p128.s2.b1: Before leaving he held a family conference, solemnly installed James, just past eighteen, as acting head of the family, and exacted promises of obedience to James from everyone. He could have walked home each night, but he purposely stayed away; his true motive was to train James and Joseph to bear the family responsibility.
p128.s2.b3: In Sepphoris he worked and lived with gentiles and made a close study of the gentile mind. But the city’s moral standards were far below those of Nazareth, and he was unwilling to be employed on public work under Herod Antipas, so he returned to Nazareth. Even then he did not take back the direction of the household, leaving it with James.
p128.s3.h: III. The Twenty-Third Year (A.D. 17) — A Journey with Simon, and a Meeting with Stephen
p128.s3.b0: With four now working, the family’s finances eased a little, and Jesus took Simon to Jerusalem by way of the Decapolis, returning by the coast road. These three weeks were the longest break from daily toil he had had since his father’s death. At Philadelphia they met a merchant from Damascus who owned over four thousand camels, and this meeting led to the episode that follows.
p128.s3.b1: In Jerusalem Jesus spent four hours with a young Hellenist named Stephen, talking about the way of life and the true God and his worship. Stephen never forgot his words; years later his bold preaching of the gospel led to his being stoned to death. The emotions aroused in Saul of Tarsus, who stood by, eventually led him to become Paul.
p128.s3.b2: Meanwhile Mary was upset to hear that in Jerusalem Jesus had spent his time visiting with strangers, especially those from far countries. The family could never comprehend his urge to know people and learn their thoughts, and Mary was slowly giving up the idea that he was a child of promise.
p128.s4.h: IV. The Damascus Episode — One of the Greatest Temptations
p128.s4.b0: Jesus spent the last four months of the year in Damascus as the merchant’s guest. The merchant proposed to found a school of religious philosophy that would outrival Alexandria, asked Jesus to head it, and brought twelve merchants and bankers to back it. The text calls this one of the greatest temptations Jesus ever faced in his purely human career.
p128.s4.b2: He never told his family about the offer and returned to his daily duties in Nazareth as if nothing had happened. The narrator explains that he deliberately kept the episodes of his life separate so that people would never connect them as the doings of one individual, for the following reasons.

head: Jesus’ intention
The danger he meant to avoid
rows: Not to build up a spectacular record of achievement
Later generations venerating the teacher instead of obeying the truth
To suppress the tendency to exalt the teacher
A religion about him becoming a competitor of the gospel of the kingdom
To be known by different titles at different times
Exerting undue influence on his family and neighbors
To wait for the response of the heart
People believing in him without the spiritual reality revealed in his teaching

p128.s4.b4: As the years passed, it became harder and harder to recognize that this man was a Son of God. He seemed just another man among men, and the Father in heaven had ordained that the bestowal should unfold in exactly this way.
p128.s5.h: V. The Twenty-Fourth Year (A.D. 18) — The Invitation from Alexandria
p128.s5.b0: In his first year of comparative freedom from family responsibility, five prominent Jews of Alexandria met him at Caesarea and urged him to become a religious teacher in their city. They warned that any Palestinian uprising would be national suicide and that Jerusalem would be destroyed. Jesus thanked them but declined, saying in substance, “⟦Q 128:5.4⟧My hour has not yet come⟦/Q⟧,” and he also refused the purse they offered.
p128.s5.b2: The six months that followed were the most uneventful of his whole career. He communed much with his Father in heaven and made tremendous progress in mastering his human mind. In December James asked to marry Esta, and Miriam to marry Jacob the stone mason; Jesus consented on condition that each first train a successor.
p128.s6.h: VI. The Twenty-Fifth Year (A.D. 19) — Jude’s Arrest, and Uncle Joshua
p128.s6.b0: With all debts paid, Jesus took his youngest brother Jude on his first visit to the temple. But Jude burst out in anger at a Roman guard who had insulted a Jewish girl and was arrested, and Jesus stayed with him in prison for two days. Before the magistrate he pleaded the case judiciously and won his brother’s release. He said nothing to the family, but three weeks later he had a long talk with Jude.
p128.s6.b1: This was the last Passover Jesus attended with any member of his family. Around this time he put sand, blocks, and stones beside the repair shop, and children flocked there and begged “Uncle Joshua” to come out and tell them a big story. His friends could hardly understand how he could swing so completely from profound discussions of politics and philosophy to the joyous play of little children.
p128.s6.b2: The Roman magistrate warned him to keep an eye on the lad, and indeed Jude caused trouble again and again through thoughtless patriotic outbursts. Yet Jude never forgot the patience and forbearance his brother-father showed throughout that ordeal. The time spent sharing his confinement lasted longer in Jude’s memory than any rebuke could have.
p128.s7.h: VII. The Twenty-Sixth Year (A.D. 20) — His Father’s House Given to James
p128.s7.b0: This year Jesus became strongly conscious of possessing a wide range of potential power, but he was fully persuaded that it was not to be used until his hour should come. The conclusion of his thinking was expressed in a prayer on the hilltop.
p128.s7.b2: The stumbling block in the family was Jude. When James and Joseph wanted to cast him out, Jesus counseled patience and persuasion by example, and that counsel prevented a break in the family. When Jude ran away, Jesus placed him in the care of a fisherman relative at Magdala, and from then on Jude worked fairly steadily.

p128.s7.b5: In November, the day after the double wedding, Jesus solemnly abdicated as head of the household and established James as “⟦Q 128:7.13⟧head and protector of my father’s house⟦/Q⟧,” while promising to send something each month until his hour should come. In this way he made ready to enter the second, home-detached phase of his adult life before beginning his public work.
p128.s8.b0: Paper 128 is a record of preparing to leave. Jesus did not abandon his family; he trained them to move slowly from dependence to independence. At the same time he declined honor, money, and institutional backing one by one, guarding his mission from becoming a religion that exalted a man.
